Isn’t it true that the general theory of relativity suggests the existence of black holes, white holes, negative value e=mc2 energy, wormholes, quantum entanglement, cosmological, constant gravitational waves, and a host of other amazing things? No. General relativity does not “suggest” any of the above. General relativity provides one thing: a set of equations that govern the behavior of the gravitational field. That’s it. End of story. R μ ν − 1 2 R g μ ν = 8 π G T μ ν . That is all. This equation has many solutions, just like Maxwell’s equations for the electromagnetic field have many solutions. Just because something is a solution of the field equations of a theory does not mean that this solution represents physical reality. Solutions for equations like this one are constrained by conditions. These could be “boundary conditions” (e.g., the expectation that the field vanishes large distances from a source). These could be symmetry conditions (e.g., the expectation that a compact mass has a spherical gravitational field that does not depend on time.) These expectations narrow down the range of solutions. So let’s pick apart the specific points listed in the question. Well, I hope my answer puts those questions into a proper perspective. We can be impressed by the magnificence of Nature and be grateful for our ability in these modern times to actually make sense of some of it without turning explanations into science-fiction fairy tales. Nothing wrong with science-fiction, mind you; my favorite genre. We just need to be careful not to confuse it with reality. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Has there been a mistake or intentional deception in the announcement of the discovery of the Higgs particle? No, there is neither a mistake nor any signs of a deception. We’re talking about a discovery that was made over 12 years ago, and has been subjected to plenty of scrutiny since. A plot like this from the CMS experiment tells the story: What it tells us is that there is a slight bump at a specific energy level (approximately 125 GeV) in what appear to be the detections of correlated pairs of photons, and that this bump is consistent with what we would predict if we had a Higgs boson with a rest mass-energy of 125 GeV, decaying into a pair of photons. This is how particle physics experiments are made. Most subatomic particles are not detected directly, because they decay rapidly. However, we know what their decay products are supposed to be, and we can compare that against experiment. Before its discovery, we did not know the mass of the Higgs boson, and while certain mass ranges were excluded, estimates ranged wildly. However, once this bump was detected, things changed. The bump is not particularly significant visually, but it is very significant statistically. Of course just because there’s a bump, we cannot be certain if it is a bump due to the Higgs boson or perhaps something else. So refined experiments look at more specific properties and correlations. For instance, was the detected particle a true scalar (like the Higgs) or perhaps a composite particle that behaves like a so-called pseudoscalar? There were additional experiments that could distinguish between the two. Other hypotheses were also discarded. So now, 12 years later, I don’t think there’s any reason to doubt the validity of this discovery, any more than we might doubt, say, the discovery of the Z boson or the top quark. One question that may not be fully settled yet is whether or not the simplest, minimalist Higgs model is the valid model, or perhaps something more complicated. It would be interesting to see if we could detect a “triple Higgs” interaction, which is a Higgs boson splitting into two Higgs bosons (or equivalently, a Higgs boson emitting or absorbing another Higgs boson).

From an outside observers point of view, a black hole never forms. The rest of the universe is an outside observer. So how can Hawking radiation ever escape to the outside universe? As others pointed out, the popular account of Hawking radiation — a pair of particles popping into existence near the event horizon, one with positive one with negative energy, the negative energy particle being “eaten” by the horizon while the other escapes — is dead wrong. In fact, we can suspect this much simply by looking at the basic features of Hawking radiation. Its characteristic wavelength is about 20 times (!) the Schwarzschild radius of the black hole. That alone should make it fairly obvious that Hawking radiation doesn’t really come from the horizon proper. Indeed, when we actually look at Hawking’s own 1974 paper (rather than his popular book) a very different picture emerges. Hawking radiation is deduced from a so-called semiclassical description of quantum fields: that is to say, quantum field theory in the curved spacetime background of general relativity. This curved spacetime background is not static. An astrophysical black hole is in a perpetual state of collapse. This creates an asymmetry between past and future. When we extend the quantum fields using the appropriate “past infinity” and “future infinity” boundary conditions, the resulting configuration is not symmetric. This yields an outgoing flow of radiation, which is what Hawking radiation really is. This radiation originates from the neighborhood of the gravitating object, and it is a result of the “gravitational vacuum polarization” that is produced by the object’s gravitational field. The presence of a horizon is not essential to this process, nor does the radiation originate from, or from within, the horizon. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Can Hawking radiation (absorption of mass by a hypothetical particle and destruction of mass by a star) occur in a neutron star? Is it possible or not and why? The answer is yes, and I can explain why both using simple reasoning and the math. On the simple reasoning side: If a black hole radiates Hawking radiation in the present, it cannot be because it’s a black hole as the black hole has not formed yet. The particles collapsing into a black hole take forever (as seen by outside observers) to reach the limit when they’d form an event horizon. This is the essence, e.g., of the famous Oppenheimer-Snyder paper that, in 1939, described for the first time this process of “continued contraction”. This also means that, at least in principle, the particles may interact with one another in the last minute, second, picosecond before forming a horizon (as measured in their own reference frame) and turn around; we can never be 100% certain that this won’t happen as the black hole has not formed yet! So perhaps it never will… yet there is Hawking radiation. But never mind the fairy tale. I hold in my hand a paper, well, a single sheet of paper really as Hawking’s paper really is short: It’s his 1974 publication in Nature, titled “Black hole explosions?” Let me quote two key sentences from this paper: “The β i j will not be zero because the time dependence of the metric during the collapse will cause a certain amount of mixing of positive and negative frequencies. […] The number of particles created and emitted to infinity in a gravitational collapse can therefore be determined by calculating the coefficients β i j . ” In short: What is needed for Hawking-radiation is not a horizon but a time asymmetry; specifically, the asymmetry due to collapse, as a result of which the past and the future are not identical. What this tells us is that any collapsing cloud of matter will emit Hawking radiation unless the collapse is halted by some interaction and the configuration becomes static. In the case of a black hole, the collapse never ends. In other cases, it may. But so long as the collapse is in-progress, Hawking radiation follows, according to Hawking’s own reasoning. Why can't an observer just inside a supermassive black hole's event horizon escape if the gravity isn't strong enough at that point to tear him/her apart? First, allow me to challenge your premise. To “tear him apart”, you don’t just need gravity; you need tidal forces, which is to say, differences in gravity. Tides happen because for instance, different parts of the Earth are different distances away from the Moon, therefore lunar gravity acts on them with different strengths. Take this to the extreme, and in the vicinity of a small black hole or a neutron star, the differences become so large, your head and your big toe will want to follow wildly different orbits… thus you get torn apart. Never mind that, you are right, in the case of a very large supermassive black hole, this does not happen. In that case, tidal forces remain weak near the event horizon. But then, it’s not tidal forces that prevent you from escaping. It’s the sheer strength of gravity, not how it varies from point to point. We can measure the force of gravity, in principle, by calculating how powerful your rocket would need to be in order to simply hover. To escape, you obviously need a rocket even more powerful than that. And guess what… at the horizon, you’d need an infinitely powerful rocket simply to hover. Yet… inside the horizon it’s not even this that prevents you from escaping. What this has to do with is not so much the strength of gravity but the nature of that event horizon. You see, so long as you are outside the horizon, the horizon remains forever in the future. At the “present” of any outside observer, the horizon will not have formed yet, no matter how long they wait. The only way for any observer to make the horizon happen is by crossing it. Otherwise, it remains forever an unattainable future moment in time. But once you cross it, something else happens. Now the horizon is part of your past. I repeat, it’s not a place that you can return to. It does not have a shape. It’s a past moment in time. To return to it, to escape, you no longer need a rocket: you now need a time machine. Which, when you think about it, makes perfect sense even from the outside observers’ perspective. Recall I mentioned that for them, the horizon remains forever in the future. So if you were to escape from the black hole, to an outside observer it would imply that you are coming back from that future. There we go again… time machine. To sum up: at the horizon, you need an infinitely powerful rocket just to hover. Beyond the horizon (which is a future moment in time until/unless you cross it, when it becomes part of your past) you would need a time machine to escape.

If black holes' horizons form infinitely far in the future, then how can they evaporate in finite time? You stumbled upon a key potential contradiction between two things: But first: it is not the horizon that evaporates. Indeed, contrary to popular explanations (including Hawking’s own, from his popular science book) the actual equations tell a different story: Hawking radiation exists because the black hole is in a perpetual state of collapse and therefore, the past and the future boundary conditions are not identical. It is this difference that manifests itself in what distant observers see as outgoing radiation. (As an important aside, it should be mentioned that the characteristic wavelength of Hawking radiation is around 20 times the Schwarzschild radius. That alone should inform us that the horizon is not the source of that radiation.) So what does this mean? Do horizons never form? Maybe. Does a collapsing, evaporating black hole leave behind a “naked singularity”? Maybe. Does something else happen? Who knows, as the final moments of a black hole’s existence take place at the Planck scale, and we know nothing about the Planck scale, especially nothing about how gravity behaves at the Planck scale. The one thing we do know is that Hawking radiation is not predicated on the present-day existence of a horizon. If it were, there would be no Hawking radiation in the first place, since the horizon, even in classical general relativity, remains forever in any outside observer’s future.

Are atheists aware that they're about to go to hell for quadrillions of years? In hell, you get tormented everyday. Suppose you are right. Suppose there is an afterlife, and a day comes when we are judged, with our souls perhaps condemned to eternity. Am I going to be judged by my deeds? Sure, I made mistakes. To quote the immortal Sinatra, regrets I’ve had a few, but then again, too few to mention. And yes, there were times when I bit off more than I could chew. But I ate it up, faced it all, and, well, did my best to stand tall. Will your favorite deity or deities then judge me by my deeds? By how I lived my life? In that case, I have little to fear. Who offers an afterlife where those who proclaim their “love of god” win because no matter what sins they commit, so long as they dutifully arrive for Sunday service, all is forgiven? Well, if that’s your deity, I say bugger him. I’d rather spend an eternity in hell than be a sycophant in a tyrant’s court. But you know what? I think you have it wrong. At least if you are of the Christian persuasion. Read some Dante. Consider what happens in his vision of hell. Compare the fate of the virtuous pagans — folks who are in hell for the sin of not acknowledging Christ, either through no fault of their own (newborn, folks who lived before Christ or in far-off lands) or folks who rejected Christ for reasons of conscience — against the fate of hypocrites, including numerous popes. The sole punishment of the virtuous pagans is that they don’t enjoy God’s presence. Otherwise, they are untouched by Satan. The hypocrites, in turn, ended up in one of the deepest pits of hell. Or going back further, think of the Old Testament, the roots of all Abrahamic religions, the story of how humans were cast out of the Garden of Eden. Humans who were created in “God’s image”, which is to say, endowed with free will. A free will that was then tested when Satan tempted them to eat the forbidden fruit: Fruit from the tree of knowledge, knowledge to tell good and evil apart. In other words: a conscience. And that’s why I do not fear your imaginary afterlife. Because even though I do not believe in deities or a supernatural afterlife, I know enough about the Abrahamic family of religions to know that God does not rule by fear. If you allow yourself to be guided by fear of hell, you are already on the wrong path, of that I am certain. And that is true whether or not God actually exists.

If you were sufficiently close to two colliding black holes, would distortions in space caused by the gravity waves be fatal (ignoring all of the other fatal phenomena like the accretion disk and tidal effects)? Well, technically yes, but by that time you are too close already and you’d be killed by those tides even in the absence of a collision and the resulting gravitational waves. [Pedantic note, with apologies: A “gravity wave” is what you see on the surface of the sea when it waves. A “gravitational wave” is a propagating change in the gravitational field away from sources.] The point is, gravitational waves are propagating changes. A single object produces a gravitational field that changes from place to place but it does not change over time in the inertial reference frame in which the object is at rest. But when we have two objects inspiraling towards each other, no such inertial frame exists. The gravitational field changes not just from place to place but also over time. These changes then ripple away towards infinity with ever decreasing amplitude, much like changes in the electromagnetic field do in response to electric charges undergoing accelerating motion. When the gravitational force changes from place to place, it represents a tidal force. Different parts of a body want to head in different directions or different rates. This can rip a body apart. There are tides near any gravitating object, and tides near a black hole can be very strong because we can get very close to a black hole (they are very compact). When the black holes inspiral, these tidal forces change. Those changes propagate. But they do not get stronger with distance, quite the contrary. And in the end, what kills us is not how the tidal forces change over time, but how strong they are in the first place. Get close enough to the black hole and you’ll find out! A little farther away, though… I once calculated that if you were about the same distance from the merger of two ~30 solar mass black holes as the Earth is from the Sun, you could actually hear the result as a loud rising then decaying sound. Yes, there can be sounds in space! Well, not exactly sounds as we know them, not a traveling longitudinal pressure wave in a medium, rather, transversal gravitational waves in the vacuum but in the end how they travel is not relevant; what is relevant is that at that distance, they are powerful enough to interact with our ears. Are ANY particles "real"? Or is every particle a excitation of some QCD field? Are protons therefore, excitations in a quark-gluon field? What about neutrinos? Yes, all elementary particles are excitations of the corresponding quantum fields. (Composite particles, like the proton, are bound states of such excitations.) But ultimately, what is “real” and what is not “real” is a metaphysical question. So let’s start with a practical definition: Something is “real” if two observers agree on it, regardless of their own motion. For instance, absolute motion is not “real”: to an observer moving along with the object, the object will appear motionless. But relative motion is “real”: If one observer sees two objects moving at different speeds and/or in different directions, all other observers will see the same. The actual values will be observer-dependent, but no observer will see these two objects as not moving relative to each other. So in this vein, are particles real? Perhaps not. The particle-content that an observer sees may depend on that observer’s motion. An observer who is accelerating in an otherwise empty universe will see Unruh radiation, photons arriving from the apparent (Rindler) horizon that characterizes his acceleration. An inertial observer will see no Unruh radiation. Actually, the picture gets more complicated, since in order to actually “see” that Unruh radiation, the observer must interact with the electromagnetic field, which ultimately involves charges, so the inertial observer now sees the accelerating observer carrying accelerating charges and thus producing electromagnetic radiation… The devil is in the details, but the end result is that the two observers’ observed particle content is not the same. On a tad more technical level, it boils down to decomposing fields using a Fourier transform. What is the basis for that transform? The decomposition is not unique when accelerating reference frames are permitted. Decompositions with respect to different reference frames correspond to different descriptions of the same field in terms of particle-content. Having said that… as I said, “real” is in the eye of the beholder. When an electron hits the fluorescent screen of an old school CRT causing a flash of light that we see… how can we possibly say that this electron is not “real”? We may know that it is “only” an excitation of the electron field, and that a rapidly accelerating observer nearby might see, e.g., additional electron-positron pairs that we don’t see, but so what? The screen flashed. That’s an event. And ultimately, events are “real”, however they are interpreted in different observer reference frames, with whatever particle content might be associated with the event in these frames.

Brian Greene said: “as particles … try to move through space, they have to burrow through the Higgs field, and that is what gives them mass”. Does that mean that particles that keep at rest in the frame of the Higgs fied are gravitationally massless? Brian Greene’s “explanation” is one of many popularizations of physics that are intended to make difficult topics accessible to the “unwashed masses” but in reality, achieve the exact opposite. I would put it in the same basket in which I put the “rubber sheet” analogy of gravity, the “expanding balloon” description of cosmic expansion, even the “miniature solar system” models of the atom. Then I would put that basket out onto the curbside for collection. No, particles do not “burrow through” anything. If they “burrowed” through anything, that would mean a loss of kinetic energy through dissipative processes. Soon enough, everything would come to a halt, floating in some sticky molasses I suppose… But no, I swear, that is not how the Higgs works. Remember that mass is energy? No, mass is not “converted” into energy or vice versa. What we call inertial mass, or rest mass, is the internal energy-content of a thing. That’s what E = m c 2 is about, not about nuclear energy or converting anything into anything: It literally tells you that mass and (internal) energy are the same thing. Equivalent. Unsurprisingly, the equation itself is called the mass-energy equivalence relationship. In the Standard Model of particle physics, most particles start off as massless particles, but they interact with the Higgs field. However, the Higgs field has a very peculiar property. In empty space (i.e., the lowest energy state achievable, the vacuum) the Higgs field itself is not “empty”, so to speak. So particles can interact with it even when there’s supposedly nothing there. In effect, particles interact with the vacuum. Interaction means potential energy. (E.g., when two objects interact by, say, repelling one another, you need to invest energy to push them together, and that energy will be “stored” as their interaction energy while they are close to each other.) When an initially massless electron, for instance, interacts with the vacuum, it means it carries that interaction energy with it, no matter what it does or where it goes. And because the vacuum is everywhere, so to speak, the electron cannot get rid of that interaction energy. It’s always there. That interaction energy shows up, for all practical intents and purposes, as part of the energy-content of that electron. And as I stated above, energy-content means inertial mass. So the electron behaves as a massive particle, because no matter where it goes, what it does, it carries along that interaction energy with the vacuum Higgs field (to be more precise, the so-called vacuum expectation value, or v.e.v., of the Higgs field). So I stress, no “burrowing” is involved. The Higgs field has no rest frame, and how fast or how slow the particle moves with respect to this non-existent rest frame is irrelevant. In its own reference frame, a particle is always at rest. But it still has inertial mass, because the potential energy of its interaction with the Higgs field is there, no matter what.

Why does the weakness of gravity prevent scientists from finding the graviton? We detect particles by detecting their interactions with other particles. The strength (or weakness) of the coupling between the particles determines the “cross-section”, basically the likelihood, that a detectable interaction occurs. When the coupling is really, really weak, such interactions occur very rarely. In a 2012 lecture[1], the late Freeman Dyson presented an interesting calculation. The Sun, on account of being hot, emits not only thermal electromagnetic radiation but also thermal gravitational radiation. The same blackbody spectrum, just gravitons, not photons. Sure, gravity is very weak compared to electromagnetism, so instead of the several hundred septillion watts that it emits in the electromagnetic spectrum, the Sun “only” emits about 79 megawatts of thermal gravitational radiation, but that is still a respectable radiating power. If we had a 79 megawatt light bulb at 1 astronomical unit (the Sun-Earth distance) from here, we’d have no trouble detecting it, and no trouble detecting individual photon events from that source using a suitable detector. But this 79 megawatts is not in the form of electromagnetic waves but in the form of gravitational waves. Now Dyson imagined using the entire Earth, every last bit of it, as kind of a “perfect” graviton detector: That is, he assumed that we can somehow monitor the entire Earth in a completely noise-free setting, and detect a single atomic transition (an electron jumping to a higher orbit) as a result of capturing a graviton. I.e., direct detection of a graviton, much the same way we can detect photons with a suitable detector. The result: Dyson’s calculation told us that we would see, on average, one such graviton event every billion years or so. That is what it means to have a very weak coupling between the gravitational field and matter. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

What are the major differences between special and general relativity and is general relativity just a final draft of special relativity? It might help to contemplate for a moment the history of the subject. In 1905, Einstein published what then became known as the theory of relativity. Its main claim was the existence of an invariant speed (which we know as the vacuum speed of light) and the resulting change in how reference frames that are in motion relative to one another are related to each other. The old, Galilean transformations between reference frames that involved absolute time were replaced by the Lorentz group of transformations according to which both space and time are measured differently in reference frames that move relative to one another. Contrary to some popular accounts, this version of relativity theory can deal with both inertial and accelerating motion. However, accelerating reference frames are “second class citizens” of the theory. They need to cope with fictitious forces such as the centrifugal force, which are absent in inertial frames. Therefore, the laws of physics are different for inertial vs. accelerating observers. Einstein’s ambition was to find a more general framework, which he referred to as the Generaltheorie, that would treat inertial and accelerating observers as equals. Early on, in what he described as his “happiest thought”, he came to the realization that such a theory necessary must involve gravity. The reason: gravity is universal. Freely falling objects near a freely falling observer will accelerate at the same rate, so from this observer’s perspective, they’d either be at rest or move at uniform velocity. Which is to say that for this observer, absent any distant points of reference, there is no difference between freefall in a gravitational field vs. floating in empty space. Thus a theory that can describe the world from the point of view of accelerating observers should automatically apply to observers in gravitational fields as well. Einstein’s effort was successful, and the general theory of relativity was born in 1915. In the absence of gravitation, the theory reduces to the “old” relativity, albeit with a more robust mathematical framework that no longer distinguishes inertial and accelerating observers. So the old, 1905 theory can be thought of as a special case, a limiting case in the absence of gravity, of the general theory. This is why the 1905 theory eventually became known as the special theory. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Can time exist without the Higgs field? Rather than trying to answer the question directly (what does it even mean for time to “exist”?) allow me to respond instead by enumerating what exists in the Standard Model of particle physics courtesy of the Higgs field. Courtesy of the Higgs field, we have massive vector bosons. As a result, only one vector boson (the photon) “survives” as a mediator of a long-range interaction (electromagnetism); interactions due to the rest, collectively labeled the “weak force”, become extremely short range, playing only a relatively marginal role in nuclear physics. Courtesy of the Higgs field, we also have charged fermions with masses. In the Standard Model, charged leptons (like the electron) and quarks start their existence as massless particles. But because of their interactions with the Higgs field’s so-called vacuum expectation value, they behave as though they were particles with nonzero rest mass, which allows, among other things, for them to form structures, including protons, neutrons, and ultimately, atoms. So without the Higgs field, we’d have no periodic table, no atoms, no matter as we know it. But “time”? All this takes place on the stage of spacetime. Particle physics exists in spacetime, with or without a Higgs field. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Why would Americans rather drive their car for days than take the train? I live in Ottawa, Canada. I occasionally visit New York City. By car, a comfortable drive with the occasional rest stops takes about 8 hours and that includes crossing the border. It's 12:30 PM right now. If I were to hop into my car at 1 PM, chances are it'd still be daylight when I get out of my car somewhere in Manhattan. Now suppose I take the train. Google Maps tells me that I could depart tomorrow at 6:07 AM and arrive in Montreal at 8:11 AM. Three hours later, I would depart on Amtrak's Adirondack train, which could deliver me at Penn station a mere 11 hours later, at 10:15 PM. OK, how about return? Well, I could board the same Adirondack train the next day at 8:28 AM, heading back to Montreal. I'd arrive at Montreal's Gare Centrale at 8:16 PM. Too bad, that's after the last train that day left for Ottawa, so I'd have to get a hotel room and board the first train next morning at 6:20 AM. I'd arrive back at Ottawa's main railway station at 8:25 AM, just three minutes short of 24 hours since my departure at Penn Station. This does not include the time it takes to get to or from the railway station but it’s thankfully short, as I live not too far from Ottawa’s main railway station. OK, I could take a plane instead. The flight time from YOW to EWR (Newark) is only 90 minutes. Of course I need to be at the airport at least maybe 2 hours early, to go through customs preclearing. And then there is the ride to/from the airport. So I’d have to leave my home at least 3 hours prior to the scheduled departure, and it’d likely take at least an hour and a half to disembark, get my luggage, get a taxi and get from the airport to Manhattan. Overall? At least 6 hours travel time if everything goes according to plan. Granted, it's a little less than the road trip, but not that much less. And far less convenient. What about environmental costs? Google tells me that with Porter Airlines, one flight option only produces 55 kg of CO2 per passenger. But that's not much less* than the CO2 I'd produce burning up less than one full tank of fuel in my Honda Accord. This gets even more pronounced if I don’t travel alone: That 55 kg is per passenger, whereas my Honda’s fuel consumption would not change noticeably just because, say, my beautiful wife joins me for the trip. Would I like to take the train to NYC? Absolutely. And a century ago, I could have. The Ottawa & New York Railway ceased operations in 1957. I could not find a timetable but I doubt travel times were any worse than traveling with VIA Rail and Amtrak these days. Probably quicker and more comfortable, as a matter of fact. But those days are gone. The railroads may have built North America but today, passenger rail service... well, sucks. *Edited: at first I thought the Honda would produce less than 55 kg, but it’s more likely 90-odd kg. Which, incidentally, is just a tad more than the per-passenger CO2 listed by Google for most flights.

What is the significance of the constant "c" in Maxwell's equations? Why does light travel at such a high speed? Whether a speed is high or low is in the eye of the beholder. Many who dream of interstellar travel think that the speed of light is way too low. But the significance? Maxwell’s equations describe the interplay between electric and magnetic fields, the former being sourced by charges and currents. There is a specific subclass of solutions to these equations in the absence of charges and currents: vacuum solutions, which turn out to be propagating plane waves. The speed of propagation corresponds to the observed electric and magnetic properties of the vacuum. Although these properties are not really properties of the vacuum per se; if we go beyond Maxwell, to quantum electrodynamics, we find that these properties are ultimately related to the “fine structure constant” (never mind the name, it has historic origins) that characterizes the strength of the electromagnetic interaction. Relativity theory is originally based on the idea that the nature of the electromagnetic interaction is the same for all observers, regardless of their motion relative to each other. This means that the speed that is derived for the electromagnetic field in the vacuum is itself an invariant speed, in fact, the invariant speed, of the theory. We can now turn the tables around and make this existence of an invariant speed a fundamental principle; we then find that any theory like Maxwell’s, which involves a “massless field”, will yield vacuum solutions that propagate at this invariant speed of relativity theory. Is this speed large? Or small? Well… how about if I told you that it is exactly 1? That is to say, anything moving at the vacuum speed of light moves exactly one “natural unit of distance” over one “natural unit of time”. So maybe the right question to ask is not why the vacuum speed of light is so high, but why the speeds in our everyday experience are so low. Why do we live in the nonrelativistic limit? I mean, imagine if we were made of stuff that exists in the deep interior of hot stars: a relativistic plasma. Particles, atomic nuclei, electrons, would all move around at relativistic speeds! The trouble is, when everything has that much kinetic energy, almost nothing sticks together. Things bounce around but do not form complex structures. If we want complex structures, we need to cool things down. Way, way down. The energies of chemical reactions are many orders below relativistic energies. When we cool things down this much, suddenly we have complexity. Chemical bonds. Complex molecules. Life. Think about it for a moment. If you were transported to the interior of a star, you would not know it. Before any sensation could reach your brain, your entire body would cease to exist, effectively instantaneously. Contrast this with being transported into deep space, far from any heat or light source. It would not be a pleasant experience to be sure, but you would stay alive, even conscious and able to function, for several seconds! Your physical body is far, far more compatible with the emptiness of space than with the high temperature environment of a star (need not even be relativistic temperatures). So there. It’s not the speed of light that is fast. It is us, nonrelativistic creatures, living on the edge of empty space and absolute zero, who are slow. Really, really, really slow. The upside of it (yes, there is an upside) is that we probably live a lot longer as a result. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

If there is a very, very tall tower, and a light source that spins around the top of it at a very high speed, would the shadow it casts ever be able to move faster than the speed of light? Indeed, shadows, spots of light, even the start of the gap in a ginormous pair of scissors can move faster than the vacuum speed of light. So in theory, with a large enough laser pointer moving fast enough, you could create a spot of light on the surface of the Moon that moves around at a speed many times greater than the vacuum speed of light. Shadows can do this, too; in fact, when we infer, for instance, the existence of a planet orbiting another star when it briefly transits in front of that star, the shadow of that planet traverses our solar system typically much faster than the vacuum speed of light, as it crosses the Earth’s orbit. There is one common theme in these examples. None of them can carry energy-momentum or information from point A to point B. You can make a laser spot traverse the Moon very fast, but two astronauts standing on the lunar surface will not be able to manipulate that spot and use it to send messages to one another. There is another thing that can travel faster than the vacuum speed of light: light! That is to say, the so-called phase velocity of light. In some ionized mediums with an index of refraction less than one, the phase velocity is greater than c . But again, the phase velocity is not something that can be used to carry a useful signal. When electrons become entangled, are they entangled forever (isn't that romantic?); or will they entangle with other electrons willy nilly (isn't that promiscuous?). When you think about entanglement, keep in mind how badly words can mislead us. Normally, everything is entangled with everything else. When we say that we entangled two particles, what we really mean is that, however briefly (within the constraints of the experiment), but we managed to keep those two particles isolated from the rest of the universe as much as possible. So at least temporarily, they were only entangled with one another, with minimum interference from the environment. Thus, the two-particle system can act as an isolated quantum system, not interacting with other things. So when electrons become entangled, they just continue what they’ve been doing all along, staying entangled. But (briefly) they’ll remain mostly unentangled with other things. What is m in f=ma, rest mass, inertial mass, variable mass, or gravitational mass? Such an old question, yet without a decent answer! The mass in F = m a refers to inertial mass. Inertia characterizes a body’s resistance to a force. You can see how when you divide this equation throughout by the mass m : a = F / m . Which is to say that given a force, a body’s resulting acceleration is proportional to that force, but inversely proportional to the body’s mass. The greater the mass, the smaller the acceleration: a body with more mass has more inertia, more resistance to motion. The term “rest mass” is synonymous with inertial mass. Consider, in fact, the title of Einstein’s famous 1905 E = m c 2 paper, which reads in English: Does the inertia of a body depend upon its energy-content? This paper establishes the equivalence of energy-content and inertia(l mass). The term “rest mass” means the same as inertial mass. It came into usage along with another term, “relativistic mass”, which combines the inertial mass of a body (which is an intrinsic property) and its kinetic energy (which is observer-dependent). Fortunately this concept is not much used anymore as it is grossly misleading and has been the source of much confusion. I am guessing that “variable mass” in the question may have referred to this relativistic mass. Gravitational mass measures how a body interacts with the gravitational field. According to the weak equivalence principle, gravitational mass and inertial mass are identical. This is what allowed Einstein to generalize his original relativity theory (now called special relativity) and extend it to become a field theory of gravitation. A theory that treats inertial and accelerating reference frames the same way (Einstein’s original objective) naturally becomes a theory of gravitation when the reference frame associated with falling in a gravitational field does not depend on the material properties of the falling object. So to sum up, the mass m in F = m a is inertial mass; it is the same as rest mass; thanks to the weak equivalence principle, it’s the same as gravitational mass; as to the concept of variable (relativistic) mass, the best advice I can offer is to forget you ever heard about such a thing. If we ever discover something that defied the laws of physics, would we be adding a new topic in physics or questioning whether or not our laws and ideas in physics were all wrong? Throughout the history of modern science, progress was made when we discovered something that defined the laws of physics known at the time. These challenges were met by making sense of what we saw, and ultimately, revising and improving our understanding of Nature. The “laws of physics” are not dogma, not some unchanging commandments from the deities of the physical sciences or anything like that. They simply reflect our present understanding of how Nature works. Challenges are welcome, especially when they are unexpected, as it is thanks to those challenges that progress is made. No, progress does not mean questioning whether our ideas “were all wrong”. We know that they are not all wrong: our ideas have been well tested through observation and experiment and they have a very good track record, successfully predicting results. So they cannot be “all wrong”. That does not mean that they are the final word on any particular topic. Take classical mechanics, for instance. It all seemed so nice and simple, back in the 18th century. But then, those pesky engineers invented steam engines. Engines producing mechanical energy out of… what exactly? Heat? What is heat? How is it related to motion? It took decades before physicists began to make sense of all this, after exploring some remarkable detours, eventually discarding concepts like caloricum and finally arriving at modern formulations of axiomatic thermodynamics and statistical physics. Or how about the luminiferous ether theory, which made perfect sense in light of Maxwell’s equations… that is, until it didn’t, in light of the famous (and, by the standards of the day, very surprising) Michelson-Morley null result, eventually leading to relativity theory? Or how about Rutherford’s surprising result? Bombard a thin gold foil with alpha particles. They should pass through with minimal deflection, according to the then-popular model of the atom, Thomson’s. But they didn’t. Some of the alpha particles were actually reflected! To quote Rutherford, “It was almost as incredible as if you fired a 15-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you.” And sure, it led to a major revision of our understanding of atoms, another step in the early 20th century towards modern particle physics. So you see, surprising discoveries happen all the time. We love them! They let us learn something new. As to how we respond to them, it depends on the nature of the discovery. Sometimes, it opens a whole new chapter in physics (e.g., thermodynamics, relativity theory, quantum theory). Sometimes it leads to a refinement or improved understanding within an existing framework (e.g., Rutherford’s atomic model). In all cases, it means we can take another meaningful step forward. What happens to matter when it falls into a black hole? Is it destroyed or stored as energy? Can you provide an explanation for this phenomenon? The problem with questions like this can be summed up with that one word used in the question itself: “when”. You see, a black hole is not just some physical object that exists here and now. We are talking relativity theory here, after all, extreme relativity, with both space and time involved. How much time? Well, that’s the tricky part. The closer something gets to a black hole, the stronger the gravitational field in its vicinity. And a strong gravitational field means time dilation. Not just minute time dilation, mind you, like here on the surface of the Earth, where clocks one part in a billion, give or take, slower compared to clocks in deep space. Extreme time dilation. Long story short, concerning that “when”: The question as to when an object falls into a black hole is answered, for us outside observers, by a simple word: never. That is to say, near the black hole’s event horizon, time dilation becomes divergent. Infinite. The moment when an infalling object would reach the event horizon remains forever in the future for outside observers. What about infalling observers? Well, they’d find themselves in a collapsing mini-universe, consisting of all things that ever fell, ever will fall into the black hole. This universe has a (very) finite lifespan. The famed singularity? That’s not some place you can avoid. It’s the future moment in time when this mini-universe comes to an end. But for outside observers, that never happens. Stuff falling into a black hole never reaches that black hole. In fact, this is precisely why black holes, in some of the older or foreign literature, were often called “frozen stars”. So in a very real sense, all that matter is still there, in the process of falling. Invisible to us due to the same time dilation that causes extreme redshift, so any signal from infalling matter is shifted into oblivion. So the black hole, for all intents and purposes, appears “black” (that is, not visible) but we know, assuming that our math is correct, that it represents a state of continued collapse (the title of the famous 1939 Oppenheimer-Snyder paper, which first described such collapse, reflects this: On Continued Gravitational Contraction.) How do you know there is no speed of gravity? For the same reason I know there is no speed of water. I look at a glass of water, and it’s perfectly still. I look at a fast-flowing river, and the water is moving, well, very fast. I look the icy moon Europa of the planet Jupiter, and I see tremendous quantities of water ice moving very, very fast around Jupiter. Or maybe not moving at all if I happened to stand on Europa’s icy surface? So what exactly is the speed of water? On the other hand, I do know, for instance, the speed at which certain influences travel in water. Though it is affected by things such as temperature or salinity, sound travels roughly 1.5 kilometers a second in water. That is true in the glass of water I hold in my hands, it is true in the rivers and oceans, it is even true on Europa. So then, gravity. A static gravitational field has no speed. Why would it? Speed measures change. There is no change when the field is static. However, if you are wondering how fast changes in the gravitational field travel, far from any specific source of gravitation: Why, it’s the same speed at which changes in the electromagnetic field travel, far from any sources (electric charges). It’s called the vacuum speed of light, light being the word we associate with a particular range of frequencies of electromagnetic waves, which also include radio waves, infrared and ultraviolet light, X-rays and gamma rays. Similarly, changes in the gravitational field travel in the form of waves, and far away from sources (masses), those waves are transverse waves traveling at the same vacuum speed of light. But that is not the “speed of gravity” any more than the speed of light is the “speed of electromagnetism”. Forgive the pedantry here, but it is important to convey the correct impression: namely that speed is associated with the rate at which changes travel, the static field itself has no speed associated with it.

Which one is more dangerous, antimatter or black holes? Dangerous in what sense? I mean, look. Water is dangerous. You fall off a bridge into an icy river, you die. You fall off a ship in the middle of the ocean, you die. Oxygen is dangerous. It corrodes just about anything and everything, in some cases rather explosively. One careless act inside a wood frame house and you die a horrible, fiery death. Cats are dangerous. These cuddly little guys can give you scratches, can bite you, cause a wound to be infected, and if you’re not careful, you might even die. They can also carry rabies. Antimatter? Take a banana. It is slightly radioactive because it contains the naturally occurring radioactive isotope, potassium-40. These atoms decay, and rarely, maybe once in 100,000 decaying atoms, the decay produces a positron: the antimatter partner of the electron. Now, do you feel that you are in any danger in the presence of a banana because it emits a steady stream of antimatter particles? And then, black holes. Well… the nearest known black hole is a tad over 1500 light years away. That’s close to 300,000 times the distance from the Earth to the Sun. That particular black hole not particularly large insofar as black holes are concerned, only about 10 times the mass of the Sun. Dangerous? Well, let’s say you approach the Sun to within a distance of 1 million kilometers. Guess what… you’ll be fried to a crisp. At that distance, you’ll be exposed to 30 megawatts of thermal energy per square meter. For comparison, your kitchen oven uses a few kilowatts, no more. So it’s like being surrounded by several thousand kitchen ovens, all turned up to the maximum, dumping all that heat on you. I daresay that qualifies as dangerous, perhaps extremely so. In contrast… say, you approach a quiescent black hole of 10 solar masses within a distance of 1 million kilometers. What will you see? Nothing, really. Assuming your spaceship or spacesuit are functioning well, you’ll be happily floating in empty space, and as for the black hole, even if you knew where to look and had a decent telescope, it’d only appear as a very mild distortion of the starfield behind it. We can, of course, look at things from a statistical perspective. According to some US statistics (though I suspect other countries’ statistics would appear quite similar) poisoning is by far the greatest danger, causing some 45% of accidental deaths in 2022. Falls are next (20%) followed by motor vehicle accidents (also 20%), suffocation (3%), other injuries (2%), drowning (2% — see? I told you water is dangerous!), fire (1% — darn that oxygen) and then other, more minor causes. What I don’t see on this list is antimatter or black holes, neither of which, to the best of my knowledge, ever caused any harm to a human, one (antimatter) on account of its rarity, the other (black holes), on account of its distance and, well, benign nature compared to a hot, burning star for instance. Is there any visible light from the Big Bang or just radiation? If there is visible light, what color would it be and why? If not, how do we know that the Big Bang occurred? If by “Big Bang”, we mean the presumed initial moment of the universe, there is no light, radiation, or anything from this moment. And we do not know if such a moment occurred or not. But that is because the unfortunately named (let’s not forget, the expression was coined by one of the theory’s critics, the astronomer Sir Fred Hoyle, back in 1949, when he was an advocate for an alternative, “steady state” cosmological model) “Big Bang paradigm” is not about any big bangs, really. It’s about the recognition that we live in an expanding cosmos, and the science of extrapolating backwards, based on what we know about gravitation and particle physics, trying to reconstruct the universe’s past history. We can go back to when the universe was presumably 385,000 years old, give or take, and it first became transparent to its own incandescence. This white light, which was emitted everywhere in every direction, can be seen today as the microwave background radiation. Wherever you look in the cosmos, behind everything else you see a distant patch of gas, emitting light; except that this light, its wavelength increased by more than a thousandfold by cosmic expansion, is only detectable by antenna as radio waves. We can go back further, based on science that we know, science that we tested in the laboratory, in large particle accelerators. In fact, we can go back to when the universe was roughly 1 picosecond old, and the conditions resembled the highest-energy collisions in the Large Hadron Collider. But no further. Speculating beyond that is truly pointless. We have no data, no basis for comparison. Was that first picosecond really a picosecond? Or an eternity? Was there a “before” or was there truly a singular beginning and talking about “before” is like asking about Santa’s home a mile north of the North Pole? We simply don’t know. But we do know that we live in an expanding universe and that in the distant past, the universe was hot and dense. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Is it a coincidence that all particles with Higgs mass carry electric charges? Not sure if I’d call it a coincidence, nor is it, strictly speaking, true. Yes, the Higgs mechanism is responsible for the rest masses of all charged fermions (charged leptons and quarks). Why not neutrinos? Well, neutrinos need a different mechanism that yields the so-called mass mixing matrix, which is the secret behind the observed neutrino flavor oscillations. The Higgs mechanism is also responsible (albeit in a different way) for the masses of the electroweak vector bosons, but here, we have both the charged W-bosons and the neutral Z-boson. So there, there’s a particle that is massive thanks to the Higgs but has no electric charge. So perhaps a pertinent question is not so much why the Higgs prefers charged particles (since most elementary particles are charged) but why neutrinos have such weird behavior when it comes to mass. Can Schrodinger's equation be proven to accurately describe quantum mechanics? Are there alternative methods for dealing with quantum mechanics? Schrödinger’s equation defines nonrelativistic quantum mechanics. It can be deduced from the classical Hamiltonian, or from the canonical commutation relation p q − q p = − i ℏ , but either way: nonrelativistic quantum mechanics is Schrödinger’s equation. It’s not “proven” (never will be) beyond showing that the math is self-consistent; is is validated when experiments confirm the equation’s predictions. There are, of course, alternatives. There is relativistic quantum particle mechanics in the form of Dirac’s equation. There is relativistic quantum field theory, which kind of implies either the Dirac or the Schrödinger equation in the appropriate limit. And then there are tentative theoretical approaches that attempt to generalize the commutation relation, e.g., by introducing a length scale. The Dirac equation and quantum field theory (in the form of the Standard Model of particle physics) are mathematically self-consistent and are validated by experiment. Alternatives, not so much. Even when the math itself is robust, there is no validation in the form of observational evidence. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

When and why does semi-classical gravity break down? Does it? Does semiclassical gravity break down? This is not a facetious question on my part. Semiclassical gravity works. It covers all regimes that are accessible to us, and all regimes that will likely ever be accessible to us, through observation and experiment. Semiclassical gravity amounts to the ad hoc replacement of the classical stress-energy-momentum tensor T μ ν in Einstein’s field equations with the expectation value ⟨ T ⟩ μ ν of its quantum field theory counterpart: R μ ν − 1 2 R g μ ν = 8 π G ⟨ T ⟩ μ ν . There. This equation works here, works in the laboratory, works in the bulge of the Milky Way, works near black holes, including phenomena predicted, like Hawking radiation, and phenomena observed, like gravitational radiation from inspiraling black holes or neutron stars. We are not happy with it. It’s inelegant. It is incompatible with at least some interpretations of quantum physics, notably those that, on some level, treat wavefunction collapse as an actual physical phenomenon. But mostly, it’s unsatisfying. Why can’t we quantize gravity? If it’s not a quantum theory, what’s behind this expectation value business? What justifies its use in the field equations? It is presumed that this equation ceases to be valid at or near the Planck scale. In fact, many assume that quantum field theory itself is just an effective theory that becomes invalid at the Planck scale. But for now, I’d say, the case remains open. Semiclassical gravity works. The possibility is there that it represents (at least insofar as we can discover it, given the observations that we can make in a 14 billion year old universe) the final word that we can ever say on the subject outside the realm of mathematically inspired, but observationally unconfirmed speculation. Why is light a particle and a wave at the same time? Can you explain the two slot experiment? “Wave-particle duality” is another one of those unfortunate phrases that are invented to help explain a difficult concept, but do more harm than good in the end. So here is the thing when it comes to quantum phenomena: the exact outcome of a measurement, carried out using a classical instrument (say, the human eyeball) cannot be predicted. We can only predict probabilities. But it’s not like “classical” probabilities. The limitation does not arise from the fact that we lack full knowledge of the system. Rather, the exact outcome of an experiment does not exist until, well, until it exists. It is not some technological limitation: it is not predictable in principle. But then… what can we predict? We can predict probabilities. And these probabilities are governed by an equation that, for all practical intents and purposes, travel like a wave. Waves that interfere with one another. Waves that reinforce or cancel one another at various places. In the end, though we do not observe these waves. We observe, say, the impact of a photon. There! A particle, making its appearance at a specific place, say, a specific point on your retina when you see a brief flash of light. But “en route”, there was no particle. We cannot identify the path that the particle traveled in order to reach its destination because no such path exists. What we can do is explore that “probability wave” as it “travels” from source to destination. This allows us to assign specific probabilities as to where the “particle” might be observed when it comes to that. So you see… that thing we observe is really not a particle: a particle, like a miniature cannonball, would follow a well-defined trajectory, and in this case, no such trajectory exists. But that thing we observe is really not a wave either. The “wave” in question is a mathematical abstraction, a probability amplitude, not a “thing”. The “thing” is the impact of the photon on your retina, which is particle-like behavior, but again, a true particle would have a path associated with it. And it is this point that I need to offer a reminder that, like it or not, quantum physics cannot be intuited. It is outside the ability of the human mind to intuit these things, just as, say, a language model like GPT cannot “intuit” an image or a sound, as it lacks the ability to process images or sounds. It can still reason about them, but that reasoning requires discipline and, well, knowledge of mathematics. We are in the same shoes here: With our scientific discipline and mathematical tools, we can make robust predictions about the quantum world. But we make these predictions precisely because we let go of our desire to intuit the quantum world and instead, chose to follow the math (verified by experiment, of course). So that’s my advice: Do not take this “wave-particle” business literally, as an invitation to try to intuit the unintuitable. Or if you must, at least remind yourself that the “wave” is a probability wave (not a physical thing), and the “particle” is not really a particle with a definite path, even if in the end, when we observe it (but only then!) it may masquerade as one. At 0 Kelvin, the motion of particles is completely halted. But is there a phase, under some circumstances, where the subatomic particles (electrons) also stop moving? Sigh. You received many answers to this years-old question, but several of them seem united in terms of a key misunderstanding: "particles" are not miniature cannonballs and the classic concept of "motion" does not apply. But first of all, it's important to note that 0 K is not an achievable state. It is a consequence (or if you wish, a particular restatement) of the third law of thermodynamics. Having said that, the meaning of 0 K for a system is that it is in its unique lowest energy or ground state. It is not about motion or the absence of motion, it is about the fact that no lower energy state exists: The system can only receive energy by interacting with other systems, it can no longer transfer energy to those other systems. To elaborate further, think what thermal equilibrium means. You bring two systems into contact, energy flows from the warmer to the colder system until the two have the same temperature. At that point, the transfer of energy ceases. Now a system that is at absolute zero does not have any energy left to transfer to other systems; it can only receive energy from other systems if brought into contact with them. This statement remains valid in both classical and in quantum physics, but the meaning is different. If the world consisted of classical particles, miniature cannonballs, absolute zero would indeed mean that all motion ceases, and the system has no residual potential energy either that could bring parts of it into motion. In the case of quantum systems, the concept of "motion" may lose its meaning completely (atoms are not miniature solar systems with electrons orbiting!) but the basic concept remains the same: Absolute zero means that the system can only receive energy from other systems as it comes into equilibrium with them, it cannot release energy. Lastly, this has nothing to do with the uncertainty principle. Some characterized it as a limitation of our knowledge of particle positions and velocities. That is nonsense. As I said, particles are not miniature cannonballs. Their positions and momenta have no classical analogies. They are described mathematically by “non-commuting” entities, which is to say, their values are not at all like the ordinary number-valued positions that we are used to in the classical world. Sorry, we cannot intuit this. Math is needed. Suffice to say, it means that if one of these quantities, say, the position is momentarily number-valued, the other cannot be number-valued at the same time. The “particle” simply does not HAVE a classically meaningful position and velocity at the same time. But again, while this explains why I stressed the point that quantum particles are not miniature cannonballs, the thermodynamic principles here are equally valid in the classical and the quantum world. Quantum physics is not required to elaborate on the generic concept of a lowest energy state. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

How do we obtain covariant matrix from contravariant matrix? Is the product of contravariant metric tensor and covariant metric tensor equal to kronecker delta? Indeed, the inner product of the covariant and the contravariant forms of the metric yield the Kronecker-delta: g μ ν g ν κ = δ κ μ . Matrices are (or rather, can be) representations of tensors in a specific coordinate system. There is no such thing as a “covariant matrix” or a “contravariant matrix”. If we wanted to be absolutely pedantic about it, a covariant rank-2 tensor should be represented by a row of rows (i.e., a matrix of only one row, with its elements themselves row vectors) and a contravariant rank-2 tensor would be a column of columns; only a mixed-index tensor could be represented properly by a matrix of numbers. But we “cheat” and use matrices anyway for both covariant/contravariant and mixed-index tensors, dropping a bit of pedantic rigor for the sake of convenience. In any case, the general rule is that we use the metric to raise and lower indices, i.e., turn something covariant into something contravariant and vice versa. So to turn a contravariant rank-2 tensor into a covariant one, we’d need to multiply by the covariant metric tensor twice: A μ ν = g μ κ g ν λ A κ λ . So then, if we choose to forego pedantry and represent g μ ν and A κ λ as matrices g and A , it would amount to multiplying A by g on the left and the transpose of g on the right: A ′ = g ⋅ A ⋅ g T , where I used A ′ for the matrix representing A μ ν . Of course the metric is (usually) symmetric, so g = g T . If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

If the constant G has an uncertainty of about 10^-15 m3 kg-1 s-2 why is the terrestrial GM product known to an accuracy of 10 digits m3 s-2? Be careful not to put the cart before the horse. The “standard gravitational parameter”, G M , of a celestial body can be directly measured. If you observe the orbit of a satellite around the Earth, or the orbit of a planet around the Sun, you get an extremely precise value of G M . For instance, for the Sun, the value of G M is known to better than 11 significant digits! However, just because we know G M does not mean we know either G or M . And this is the root of the problem. We cannot just take the Earth and put it on a scale, measuring its mass. Nor can we do the same with the Sun. We can measure smaller masses directly, but smaller masses have very weak gravity, and in that cause, the gravitational force itself is so weak, any measurement of G M will necessarily be imprecise. So we either measure G M precisely but only guess M ; or we can measure M accurately, but G M very crudely. Either way, we can only infer G = G M / M , because there is no way to measure G directly. Which is why, insofar as G is concerned, four decimals is pretty much the best that we can do at present. And yes, this means that we only know the masses of celestial bodies like the Sun, the Earth, the planets do this accuracy, even though we know their standard gravitational parameters, the respective values of the product G M , very precisely. Why doesn’t the Higgs field impart mass to a stationary photon? Is it theHiggs field that gives the photon mass while it is moving? The answer is… a tad complicated. The Higgs field imparts mass on certain particles indirectly through two distinct mechanisms, both of which are linked to a fundamental property of the Higgs field: Its self-interaction potential. Without going into details, for most fields, the lowest-energy state is when the field is free of excitations. For instance, the electromagnetic field is in its lowest-energy state when there are no photons (which are the excitation quanta of the electromagnetic field). Not the Higgs field. Its lowest energy state is when some excitations are present. This is what is expressed through the famous “Mexican hat” potential that are sometimes shown in popular science publications. What this means in practice is that the “vacuum” in which the Higgs field is free of excitations is not really the vacuum: It can decay into a lower-energy state, in which the Higgs field has some excitations. This lowest energy state is what we know as the vacuum. This has two consequences. First, the Higgs field interacts with certain particles (charged fermions) directly. This means that in this new, lowest-energy vacuum, the nonzero excitations (nonzero vacuum expectation value, or v.e.v.) of the Higgs field interacts with those fermions (electrons, quarks, etc.) An interaction means energy, energy means mass… so those fermions, which were initially massless in the theory, now behave as though they had mass all along, carrying this interaction mass-energy as their rest mass. There is another class of particles, vector bosons, which mediate what is known as the “electroweak” force: a unification of the electromagnetic and weak forces. There are four such vector bosons, and they form a particular symmetry group that combines three of the four, while the remaining one has its own, different symmetry group. When the Higgs field leads us to that new, lower-energy vacuum state that I described earlier, the symmetry group of the three vector bosons gets broken. In practice, this manifests itself in the form of interactions that, again, show up as rest mass-energy for these three vector bosons (these are the bosons of what we know as the weak interaction, namely the Z, W+ and W- bosons). However, the photon is unaffected by this symmetry breaking. Higgs or no Higgs, it remains massless, because its unique symmetry group is different in nature, and not sensitive to the Higgs-induced symmetry breaking (it’s a so-called Abelian group). As I said… the answer is a tad complicated. I hope it’s not completely incomprehensible, though.

Is a single electron considered an actual particle in quantum mechanics, or is it always just a wave packet with definite properties at any given time? Oh, in quantum mechanics, a particle like an electron is always a particle, an actual, immutable particle. The waves (which is to say, the wavefunction) determine the physical properties, including the position and momentum of this particle. In the Copenhagen interpretation, this wavefunction is interpreted as a probability amplitude, and it is used in conjunction with the concept of an idealized, classical measurement apparatus, to compute the probability of finding the electron somewhere, or moving with some momentum. In quantum field theory, there are no particles, only fields. The fields are quantum fields, which is to say, just like the position of that poor electron in quantum mechanics, the field does not have definite values at specific places and times; rather, a wavefunction determines (at least in the Copenhagen interpretation) the probability of finding the field with specific values at specific places and times. However, another property of these quantum fields is that when they interact, their values go up or down one unit at a time. It is these unit excitations that we observe, in localized interactions, with particle-like behavior. So to sum up/reiterate, in quantum field theory, an electron is an excitation of the corresponding fermionic field (the electron field). The wavefunction (not to be confused with the field proper) may be interpreted as a probability amplitude that tells us the probabilities of finding the field in a definite state using a classical instrument. Interactions between fields create and destroy excitations (“particles”). In contrast, in quantum mechanics particles are eternal, there are no fields, and the wavefunction can be interpreted as a probability amplitude that tells us the probability of finding the particle in some state somewhere using a classical instrument. Were the space shuttles capable of aborting a descent from orbit and re-establishing that orbit? That might have saved the Columbia shuttle if it were possible. No, unfortunately that’s not the way it works. Let’s do a teeny bit of math. What do you think requires more energy? To lift a spacecraft to an altitude of around 400 kilometers, where the ISS orbits, or to accelerate the spacecraft to orbital speed? Well, the gravitational potential energy can be estimated crudely using E = m g h . Let’s just use g = 10  m / s 2 , and we get about 4  M J for every kilogram of spacecraft. Kinetic energy, in turn, is E = 1 2 m v 2 , and orbital speed is roughly 8  k m / s . So that would be roughly 32  M J . In other words, almost 90% of the energy spent to launch that shuttle was used to accelerate it, not to lift it. Now about that re-entry. It begins with a small burn that alters the shuttle’s orbit so that it basically intersects the upper atmosphere. The atmosphere does the rest, slowing the spacecraft down. All that kinetic energy (almost as much energy as that of a small nuclear bomb!) is converted into heat, which is why there is a need for some really serious thermal shielding. Returning from a partial descent to orbit would have required another large fuel tank like the one the shuttle used for its initial ascent. In other words, no, that is not possible. And what would have been accomplished by that anyway? The shuttle had limited consumables on board. It had to return. No, what might have saved Columbia was immediate action upon observing the foam impact during ascent. Taking the concerns seriously instead of dismissing their significance. Letting the astronauts know what they face. Authorizing impromptu repairs, even though the probability of success was low. Accelerating the preparations to launch Atlantis, while saving consumables on board Columbia as much as possible, to prolong the mission. All these options were risky of course, but they could have turned a disaster into a success, just as decades prior, the Apollo 13 disaster was turned into a spectacular, historic success by luck, clever engineering and perseverance. Then again, this is all hindsight. What if nothing had happened and Columbia survived re-entry with only minor damage? Nobody would even remember STS-107. It would be a minor footnote somewhere, something to the effect of, “STS-1xx was delayed due to extensive repairs required by Columbia after its left wing was damaged during launch of the STS-107 mission and suffered further damage upon re-entry. Launch procedures were adjusted to reduce the chances of a similar debris impact in future missions.” Sadly, that’s not what happened and seven brave souls were lost, along with a magnificent flying machine. It was eerie to watch images on CNN like the one below. As far as I can recall, these images were broadcast live (courtesy of WFAA I believe), so we CNN viewers already knew that something awful happened, even while NASA engineers were still desperately trying to reach Columbia through backup radio channels. “Columbia, Houston. UHF comm check…”

Could a device be invented that synchronizes the flow of time between vastly different gravitational fields, standardizing time measurement across space? The answer is a flat no, but behind this answer lies an understanding of what time really is. I mean, in practical terms, not hifalutin’ philosophy. That is to say, what we measure as time in this one-and-only physical universe in which we, for better or for worse, live. One observed property of this physical universe is that in it there are things that tick. Not only do they tick, they tick reliably. Which is to say, if you have two such things, they will tick at the same rate. And even if you take them on distant journeys, when you bring them back together, they’ll still be ticking at the same rate. We call these things reliable clocks. It does not matter if they are cesium atoms or grandfather clocks. The only thing that matters is that they tick reliably, and they are reliably identical. Now you take two of these things and start counting the ticks. Then you let them off on different journeys. When you bring them back together, they’ll still be ticking in synch, but you will find that one may have counted fewer ticks than the other! And it depends on the journey it took. The one that traveled faster. Made more changes in speed or direction. The one that spent more time near heavy objects. Note that I have not mentioned any “flow of time” nor do I plan to, apart from this one mention on double quotes. There is no such thing. What there is, it’s a property associated with the paths of the respective trajectories of these reliable clocks: their world lines, that is. A kind of a “length” (though a rather non-intuitive concept of “length”) associated with these world lines. A reliable clock measures this length, called “proper time” along its world line. Different world lines have different lengths between the same points. But why is it surprising? After all, different paths between two points have different lengths in a map, too. Walking straight takes fewer steps than following a zig-zag path. Now I mentioned the proper time is counterintuitive, and it is true: Unlike lengths, proper time is the longest between two events when the clock is moving inertially, not accelerated in any way. Take two events. Say, right here, at my desk, at 6 PM tonight and at 6 PM tomorrow. My reliable clock counts exactly 86,400 ticks between these two events. But if you were to be here at 6 PM then blast off in your relativistic spaceship at high acceleration, turn around at some point, and get back at 6 PM tomorrow, your world line would have fewer ticks. The same thing happens in gravitational fields: a world line taking through a gravitational field will be measured with fewer ticks than another that takes a different path. Of course many other things affect the overall “length” of a world line, but this is the role gravitational fields play. In fact, reliable clocks can even be used to measure gravitational fields! (Today’s atomic clocks are sensitive enough to measure a difference in altitude amounting to no more than a few centimeters.) But ultimately, it’s not about any “flow of time” (sorry, I just broke my promise and mentioned it a second time). It’s about the “length”, i.e., the proper time associated with, different world lines. That proper time is the only actual concept of time that we can measure. Every other concept of time — e.g., coordinate time, “flow of time” (yikes! That’s the third time!) — is a mathematical or philosophical construct, not physical reality. Proper time is physical reality. In fact, ultimately all other measurements — measuring lengths, for instance, or speed — boil down to calibrating the measurements using reliable clocks and proper time in general relativity.
